title: Neural Network Training and Optimization
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Neural Network Training and Optimization ##### The learning rate that cost three weeks A team in Pune spent three weeks tuning a network for document classification. They tried four architectures, three regularisation schemes, and two data augmentation strategies. Validation accuracy stayed stuck around 61%. A new engineer ran a learning-rate range test on the first afternoon. The plot showed loss diverging above 3e-4 and barely moving below 1e-5. They had been training at 1e-3 — well into the divergent region — and every architecture change was being evaluated on a model that was oscillating rather than converging. Setting the learning rate to 8e-5 with a cosine schedule took accuracy to 84% in one run, with the original architecture. **The learning rate is the single most consequential hyperparameter in deep learning**, and it is routinely the last thing people tune. Today is about the optimisation and regularisation choices that determine whether a network trains at all, and about reading loss curves well enough to know which knob to turn. ##### Optimizers Three algorithms cover almost everything, and the differences between them are worth understanding rather than memorising. **SGD with momentum** accumulates a velocity vector: ``` v_t = β·v_{t-1} + g_t θ_t = θ_{t-1} − η·v_t ``` In a ravine — where one direction is much steeper than another — oscillating components cancel while the consistent along-ravine component accumulates. With β = 0.9, that gives roughly a 10× amplification along stable directions. **Adam** adds per-parameter adaptive learning rates by tracking exponential moving averages of the gradient and its square: ``` m_t = β₁m_{t-1} + (1−β₁)g_t first moment (momentum) v_t = β₂v_{t-1} + (1−β₂)g_t² second moment (scale) m̂ = m_t/(1−β₁ᵗ), v̂ = v_t/(1−β₂ᵗ) bias correction θ_t = θ_{t-1} − η·m̂/(√v̂ + ε) ``` Parameters with historically large gradients get smaller steps. The bias correction matters because both EMAs start at zero, so early estimates are biased toward zero. **AdamW** fixes how Adam handles weight decay, and the distinction is not cosmetic. ```python import torch.optim as optim # Adam with weight_decay adds the L2 term to the GRADIENT # It then flows through the adaptive scaling and gets divided by sqrt(v) optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01) # coupled # AdamW applies decay DIRECTLY to the weights, outside the adaptive machinery optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01) # decoupled ``` With coupled decay, parameters with large historical gradients receive *less* regularisation than parameters with small ones — the opposite of the intent, and the effective decay becomes unpredictable and entangled with the learning rate. **Use AdamW.** One refinement from modern training recipes: exclude biases and normalisation parameters from weight decay entirely. ```python def build_optimizer(model, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01): decay, no_decay = [], [] for name, param in model.named_parameters(): if not param.requires_grad: continue if param.ndim <= 1 or name.endswith(".bias"): # biases, BN/LN params no_decay.append(param) else: decay.append(param) return optim.AdamW([ {"params": decay, "weight_decay": weight_decay}, {"params": no_decay, "weight_decay": 0.0}, ], lr=lr) ``` | Optimizer | Converges | Generalises | Tuning effort | Use for | |---|---|---|---|---| | SGD + momentum | Slower | Often **best** | High (LR-sensitive) | Vision, when you can tune | | Adam | Fast | Good | Low | Prototyping | | **AdamW** | Fast | Good | Low | **Default choice** | | RMSprop | Fast | Moderate | Low | RNNs, legacy code | The honest note: **well-tuned SGD with momentum frequently generalises better than AdamW** on computer vision tasks, which is why most published ImageNet results use it. AdamW is the better default because it works well with less tuning. ##### Learning rate schedules Constant learning rates are almost never optimal. Large steps explore; small steps refine. ```python epochs, steps_per_epoch = 100, len(train_loader) # Cosine annealing — the modern default optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, T_max=epochs, eta_min=1e-6) # One-cycle: warm up then anneal, often the fastest to converge optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR( optimizer, max_lr=1e-3, steps_per_epoch=steps_per_epoch, epochs=epochs, pct_start=0.3, anneal_strategy="cos", div_factor=25, final_div_factor=1e4, ) # NOTE: steps per BATCH, not per epoch # Reduce on plateau — adaptive, needs no schedule design optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(optimizer, mode="min", factor=0.5, patience=5, min_lr=1e-7) # Warmup then cosine — standard for transformers from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import LambdaLR import math def warmup_cosine(optimizer, warmup_steps, total_steps, min_ratio=0.05): def lr_lambda(step): if step < warmup_steps: return step / max(warmup_steps, 1) progress = (step - warmup_steps) / max(total_steps - warmup_steps, 1) return min_ratio + (1 - min_ratio) * 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * progress)) return LambdaLR(optimizer, lr_lambda) ``` **Warmup deserves explanation** because it looks like superstition. At step 1, Adam's second-moment estimate `v` is built from a handful of samples and is extremely noisy. Dividing by `√v̂` of a bad estimate produces enormous, badly-directed steps that can destroy the initialisation — and with residual connections and normalisation layers, an early bad step is often unrecoverable. Warmup gives the estimate time to stabilise. Two scheduler gotchas. `ReduceLROnPlateau` takes a metric: `scheduler.step(val_loss)`. Every other scheduler takes nothing: `scheduler.step()`. And `OneCycleLR` steps **per batch**, so calling it once per epoch means the schedule finishes in the first few percent of training. **The learning-rate range test** is how you find the right magnitude in ten minutes rather than three weeks: ```python import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt, copy def lr_range_test(model, loader, criterion, device, start_lr=1e-7, end_lr=1.0, n_steps=200): model = copy.deepcopy(model).to(device) opt = optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=start_lr) gamma = (end_lr / start_lr) ** (1 / n_steps) sched = optim.lr_scheduler.ExponentialLR(opt, gamma) lrs, losses, best = [], [], float("inf") model.train() it = iter(loader) for step in range(n_steps): try: x, y = next(it) except StopIteration: it = iter(loader); x, y = next(it) x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device) opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) loss = criterion(model(x), y) loss.backward() opt.step(); sched.step() lrs.append(opt.param_groups[0]["lr"]) losses.append(loss.item()) best = min(best, loss.item()) if loss.item() > 4 * best: # diverged break fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5)) ax.semilogx(lrs, losses) ax.set_xlabel("learning rate"); ax.set_ylabel("loss") ax.set_title("Pick roughly one order of magnitude below the minimum") return lrs, losses ``` Read the plot: the loss falls, reaches a minimum, then diverges sharply. **Choose a learning rate about one order of magnitude below the minimum** — that point is already partly unstable, and you want the steepest region where loss is still falling reliably. ##### Weight initialisation Bad initialisation causes vanishing or exploding gradients before training begins. Consider a deep network where each layer multiplies the signal by roughly a factor `k`. After 50 layers the signal is scaled by `k^50` — at k = 0.9 that is 0.005, and at k = 1.1 it is 117. Either way, learning fails. The initialisation schemes solve this by preserving variance through the layer: ```python import torch.nn as nn def init_weights(model): for m in model.modules(): if isinstance(m, (nn.Linear, nn.Conv2d)): # Kaiming (He): for ReLU-family activations nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight, mode="fan_out", nonlinearity="relu") if m.bias is not None: nn.init.zeros_(m.bias) elif isinstance(m, (nn.BatchNorm1d, nn.BatchNorm2d, nn.LayerNorm)): nn.init.ones_(m.weight) nn.init.zeros_(m.bias) elif isinstance(m, nn.Embedding): nn.init.normal_(m.weight, mean=0, std=0.02) ``` | Scheme | Variance | Use with | |---|---|---| | **Xavier/Glorot** | `2/(fan_in + fan_out)` | tanh, sigmoid | | **Kaiming/He** | `2/fan_in` | **ReLU, GELU, LeakyReLU** | | Orthogonal | Preserves norms exactly | RNNs | | Zero | — | Biases only, never weights | **Kaiming's factor of 2 exists because ReLU zeroes half the activations**, halving the variance — the extra factor compensates. **Never initialise weights to zero.** Every neuron in a layer would compute the same thing and receive the same gradient, so they would remain identical forever. This is the symmetry-breaking problem, and it is why random initialisation is necessary rather than merely convenient. Diagnosing gradient flow directly: ```python def gradient_flow_report(model): rows = [] for name, p in model.named_parameters(): if p.grad is None: rows.append({"layer": name, "status": "NO GRADIENT"}) else: rows.append({ "layer": name, "grad_mean_abs": p.grad.abs().mean().item(), "grad_max": p.grad.abs().max().item(), "weight_mean_abs": p.abs().mean().item(), "ratio": (p.grad.abs().mean() / (p.abs().mean() + 1e-12)).item(), }) df = pd.DataFrame(rows) print(df.round(8).to_string(index=False)) return df ``` **The gradient-to-weight ratio is the useful number.** A healthy value sits around 1e-3 to 1e-2. Below 1e-6 means vanishing gradients — that layer is barely learning. Above 1e-1 means exploding gradients and you need clipping. Gradient clipping bounds the update magnitude: ```python loss.backward() total_norm = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0) if not torch.isfinite(total_norm): optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) # skip a poisoned step continue optimizer.step() ``` `clip_grad_norm_` rescales the whole gradient vector, preserving direction — almost always what you want. Log the returned norm: a healthy run shows it decaying and stabilising, while spikes to 100× the median mark exactly which batches cause trouble. ##### Batch normalisation and dropout **BatchNorm** normalises activations using batch statistics, then applies a learned scale and shift: ``` BN(x) = γ · (x − μ_batch)/√(σ²_batch + ε) + β ``` Three effects, and the third is the one people miss. It stabilises the distribution of activations across layers, it allows higher learning rates, and it acts as a **regulariser** because batch statistics inject noise that varies with which examples happen to share a batch. ```python class Block(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_dim, out_dim, dropout=0.3): super().__init__() self.fc = nn.Linear(in_dim, out_dim, bias=False) # bias is redundant with BN self.bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(out_dim) self.act = nn.ReLU() self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout) def forward(self, x): return self.drop(self.act(self.bn(self.fc(x)))) ``` Two details. **`bias=False` before BatchNorm**, because BN's β parameter already provides a learnable shift and the linear bias is redundant. And **the ordering** — Linear → BN → activation → dropout is the conventional arrangement, though BN-after-activation also works and the debate is largely settled by empirical testing on your data. BatchNorm's dependence on the batch is its weakness. At batch size 4 the statistics are noisy; at batch size 1 the variance is undefined. **LayerNorm** normalises per sample across features instead, which is why transformers use it universally: ```python nn.BatchNorm1d(features) # per feature across the batch — needs batch >= 16 nn.LayerNorm(features) # per sample across features — batch-size independent nn.GroupNorm(8, channels) # middle ground for CNNs with small batches ``` **Dropout** randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training: ```python nn.Dropout(p=0.3) # standard nn.Dropout2d(p=0.2) # drops whole feature maps in CNNs ``` Two framings for why it works. It prevents **co-adaptation** — a neuron cannot rely on a specific other neuron always being present, so each must learn something independently useful. And it approximates an **ensemble** of exponentially many sub-networks sharing weights, averaged at inference. Dropout is automatically disabled by `model.eval()`, with weights scaled appropriately. That is why you may see training accuracy *below* validation accuracy in early epochs with heavy dropout — a genuinely confusing observation with a simple explanation. **BatchNorm and dropout interact badly.** The variance shift between training and evaluation modes causes a documented mismatch. Practical guidance: use dropout after the final normalisation layer, or prefer LayerNorm, or reduce dropout when BatchNorm is present. ##### Regularisation and early stopping Ranked by typical impact: **More data** beats everything. Augmentation is the cheap version. **Early stopping** is free and should always be used: ```python class EarlyStopping: def __init__(self, patience=15, min_delta=1e-4, path="best.pt"): self.patience, self.min_delta, self.path = patience, min_delta, path self.best, self.counter, self.stop = float("inf"), 0, False def __call__(self, val_loss, model): if val_loss < self.best - self.min_delta: self.best, self.counter = val_loss, 0 torch.save(model.state_dict(), self.path) else: self.counter += 1 if self.counter >= self.patience: self.stop = True return self.stop def restore(self, model): model.load_state_dict(torch.load(self.path)) ``` Restoring the best weights matters. Stopping at epoch 60 and keeping epoch 60's weights, when epoch 45 was better, wastes the whole mechanism. **Weight decay** through AdamW, typically 1e-2 to 1e-4, excluding biases and norm parameters. **Label smoothing** prevents overconfidence and improves calibration: ```python criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1) ``` **Mixup** interpolates examples and labels, which is remarkably effective: ```python def mixup(x, y, alpha=0.2): lam = np.random.beta(alpha, alpha) idx = torch.randperm(x.size(0), device=x.device) return lam * x + (1 - lam) * x[idx], y, y[idx], lam x_mixed, y_a, y_b, lam = mixup(batch_x, batch_y) loss = lam * criterion(model(x_mixed), y_a) + (1 - lam) * criterion(model(x_mixed), y_b) ``` Note that mixup and label smoothing both soften targets — use one or tune the combination rather than stacking blindly. ##### Debugging training The diagnostic loop that turns a stuck model into a working one. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Training problem] --> B{Loss exactly constant?} B -->|Yes| C[Broken loop: zero_grad, backward, step,
or params not requiring grad] B -->|No| D{Loss is NaN or inf?} D -->|Yes| E[LR too high, log of zero,
or missing WithLogits loss] D -->|No| F{Can it overfit 8 samples?} F -->|No| G[Loop or data bug — fix before tuning anything] F -->|Yes| H{Loss oscillating wildly?} H -->|Yes| I[LR too high: run the range test, add clipping] H -->|No| J{Both curves flat and high?} J -->|Yes| K[Underfitting: bigger model, higher LR, more epochs] J -->|No| L{Train falls, validation rises?} L -->|Yes| M[Overfitting: dropout, weight decay, augmentation, early stop] L -->|No| N[Healthy — refine the schedule] ``` **Learning rate symptoms**, which is the assignment: | Symptom on the loss curve | Cause | Correction | |---|---|---| | Loss jumps to NaN within a few steps | LR far too high | Reduce 10–100×, add clipping | | Loss oscillates without decreasing | LR too high | Reduce 3–10×, run the range test | | Loss decreases then plateaus early and high | LR too high for the fine phase | Add a decay schedule | | Loss decreases extremely slowly | LR too low | Increase 3–10× | | Loss flat from step 1 | LR too low, or a broken loop | Range test first, then check the loop | The essential sanity check, worth running before every long training run: ```python def can_overfit_tiny_batch(model, loader, criterion, device, n=8, steps=300): """A correct training loop ALWAYS drives loss to near zero on 8 samples.""" model = copy.deepcopy(model).to(device) opt = optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3) x, y = next(iter(loader)) x, y = x[:n].to(device), y[:n].to(device) model.train() for step in range(steps): opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) loss = criterion(model(x), y) loss.backward() opt.step() if step % 50 == 0: print(f"step {step:4d} loss {loss.item():.6f}") ok = loss.item() < 0.01 print("PASS" if ok else "FAIL — the loop or data pipeline is broken") return ok ``` **If a model cannot overfit eight samples, no architecture or hyperparameter change will help.** The loop itself is broken, and this test finds that in thirty seconds rather than three weeks. Two further checks worth building in: ```python # Is the model learning anything beyond the class prior? baseline_loss = -np.log(1 / n_classes) print(f"random-guess loss: {baseline_loss:.4f} your loss: {initial_loss:.4f}") # These should match at initialisation. A much higher initial loss means # bad initialisation or a scaling problem. # Track activation and gradient statistics per layer hooks = [] stats = {} def make_hook(name): def hook(module, inp, out): stats[name] = {"mean": out.mean().item(), "std": out.std().item(), "dead_frac": (out == 0).float().mean().item()} return hook for name, m in model.named_modules(): if isinstance(m, (nn.Linear, nn.Conv2d)): hooks.append(m.register_forward_hook(make_hook(name))) # ... run one batch, inspect stats, then remove the hooks for h in hooks: h.remove() ``` The `dead_frac` statistic catches dying ReLUs — a layer where 90% of activations are zero is contributing almost nothing. ##### A training playbook The order to try things, which saves the most time: 1. **Run the tiny-batch overfit test.** If it fails, stop and fix the loop. 2. **Run the learning-rate range test.** Set the LR from the plot, not from a tutorial. 3. **Use AdamW with decoupled weight decay**, excluding biases and norm parameters. 4. **Add a cosine or one-cycle schedule** with warmup if the model is deep. 5. **Add gradient clipping** at norm 1.0 and log the norm. 6. **Train and read the curves.** Diagnose against the table above. 7. **If overfitting:** more data, augmentation, dropout, weight decay, early stopping — in that order. 8. **If underfitting:** raise LR first, then model capacity, then training length. 9. **Only then** change the architecture. That ordering is the point. The Pune team started at step 9 and spent three weeks there. ##### Common mistakes - Tuning architecture before tuning the learning rate. - Adam with `weight_decay` instead of AdamW. - Applying weight decay to biases and normalisation parameters. - `OneCycleLR` stepped per epoch instead of per batch. - `ReduceLROnPlateau` called without the metric argument. - No warmup on a deep network, then blaming the data for a NaN. - Zero initialisation, so every neuron in a layer stays identical. - BatchNorm with batch size 4, producing unstable statistics. - Early stopping without restoring the best weights. - Skipping the tiny-batch overfit test before a long run. ##### Hands-on Train the same network with SGD, Adam and AdamW at three learning rates each, and plot all nine loss curves on one figure. Then run the learning-rate range test and confirm it identifies the region your grid found — it should, in a fraction of the time. Add batch normalisation and dropout separately and together, measuring the effect on the train-validation gap. Finally, construct one deliberate overfitting scenario and one underfitting scenario, diagnose each from the curves alone, and fix them. For the mini-project, build a training-diagnostics notebook that systematically studies the effect of learning rate, optimizer, batch normalisation and dropout on a network. Include the tiny-batch overfit test as a gate before every experiment, learning-rate range tests, gradient-flow reports per layer, and learning-curve visualisations for every configuration. Write the results up as a **training playbook** for your team — an ordered checklist of what to try, what each symptom means, and which diagnostic distinguishes them. That document is more valuable than any single model you train, because it transfers. For the assignment, describe the symptoms of too-high and too-low learning rates on the loss curve and how you would correct each. Include the actual curves from your own runs at three magnitudes, and mark on the range-test plot where you would choose the rate and why it is below the minimum rather than at it. ##### Key takeaways - The learning rate matters more than the architecture — run the range test before tuning anything else. - Use AdamW for decoupled weight decay, and exclude biases and normalisation parameters from it. - Warmup stabilises Adam's second-moment estimate; cosine decay refines. The schedule often beats the optimizer choice. - Kaiming initialisation for ReLU networks; never zero-initialise weights, because symmetry never breaks. - Before any long run, verify the model can overfit eight samples — if it cannot, the loop is broken and nothing else will help.
